_: The desk's glossary (UX101 W5): every code and term the desk shows, in our own words. Read by src/lib/desk/glossary.ts (hover definitions, the codes' lookup) and Learn > Glossary (components/desk/glossary-page.tsx). Entry: id; name; group; def (one or two plain sentences, never a step's answer); forms (the exact written forms that hover and search find); pattern (a regex for a family of codes); derive (a family whose names come from the pack's own data: rules, tasks, documents, controls, deliverables, templates, datasets, roles); where; link (tool: a toolbar key, page: a Reference page, doc: a SITL document); inline false (a common word: found by search, never underlined in running text). Canonical organisation names are used here and swapped per learner (names.ts: localizable). Tested by glossary.test.ts: every code shape in the learner-facing text must resolve. skip: tokens that are not terms of art (a standard's number prefix, file formats, everyday abbreviations).

entries.name: Task code (F1.1, T8.1)
entries.def: Every task has a code. F is a Foundation task (weeks 1 and 2), T is any later task. The number before the dot is the week and the number after it is the task's place in that week.
entries.where: Home › My Tasks; the week overview

entries.name: Step code (T8.1-5)
entries.def: A step of a task: the task's code, a dash, then the step's number. The same code appears in the Evidence ref columns and in the work log.
entries.where: Task step list; Evidence ref columns

entries.name: Decision code (F1.1-D1)
entries.def: A decision point: a situation where you choose one of the options you are given. The code is the task's code, D, and the decision's number in that task.

entries.name: Task message code (T8.1-J1)
entries.def: A task message: a note that reaches your Inbox while you work on a task, describing a situation you have to decide. The code is the task's code, J, and the message's number.

entries.name: KR (key result)
entries.def: A key result is one measurable thing a task is judged on. A task lists KR1, KR2 and KR3 (sometimes KR4), each naming the activities that earn it, so you can see what counts before you start.
entries.where: Task card (What will I do); My Scores

entries.name: KC (knowledge check)
entries.def: A weekly knowledge check: a short open-book quiz on the week's topics. KC-08 is the check for week 8.

entries.name: FGE (Foundation Gate Exam)
entries.def: The exam at the end of the two Foundation weeks. It does not lock the tasks after it, but the certificate needs it passed. Its pass mark and attempts are on the Knowledge Checks screen.

entries.name: FEX (Final Exam)
entries.def: The exam in week 12, with a practical station, that closes the programme. Its pass mark is on the Knowledge Checks screen.

entries.name: Rule code (R04, L13)
entries.def: A numbered rule from the rule tables that a step tells you to apply. R rules are the core GRC rules; L rules are the extra ISO/IEC 27001 Lead Implementer rules.
entries.where: Learn › Rule tables; the step's Reference tab

entries.name: Start date
entries.def: The day your week 1 begins. You choose it the first time you open the desk, and every due date, the Calendar and the dates in your first task are counted from it.
entries.where: The start-date screen; Calendar; Home › My plan

entries.name: Due date and overdue
entries.def: A due date is the planned day for handing a task in, counted from your start date. Overdue is only ever said of the task you are on now, once its date has passed. Handing in late loses no marks and blocks no badge or certificate.
entries.where: Task sheet; week panel; Calendar; User Guide › Deadlines and late work

entries.name: Calendar week
entries.def: The week the calendar says it is, counted from your start date. The desk header shows it only when it differs from the week of the task you are working on, for example when you are on a week 1 task in calendar week 8.

entries.name: Catch-up (move my due dates)
entries.def: An offer shown when you are two or more weeks behind the calendar. It moves your start date so that the week you are working on starts today; every due date follows. Your work, your scores and the end of your access stay as they are.

entries.name: Access end (Access until)
entries.def: The last day you can work on the desk. It is counted from your first start date and is the one date in the programme that does not move when you move your due dates.
entries.where: The access chip in the header; Settings › Billing

entries.name: Attempt
entries.def: One timed sitting of a knowledge check or an exam. An attempt is used only when you press Start, each attempt draws a new set of questions, and your best attempt is the one that counts.

entries.name: Pass mark
entries.def: The score an exam needs to count as passed. The weekly knowledge checks are practice and have none; the two exams have one each, shown on the Knowledge Checks screen.

entries.name: Control sprint
entries.def: A control sprint is one task's batch of ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls that you put through the same questions and record in the tracker. There are 13, and together they cover all 93 controls.

entries.name: SPR-nn (sprint dataset)
entries.def: The dataset for control sprint nn: what the office was found to be doing for each control in that sprint. It is synthetic (made up) data.

entries.name: CIT (control implementation tracker)
entries.def: The control implementation tracker is one sheet you fill for the controls of a sprint: owner, status, maturity level, evidence reference and the next action. CIT-S8 is the tracker for sprint 8.

entries.name: LI-A (evidence pack)
entries.def: The Lead Implementer task library: for each control, a page with what it requires and small sub-tasks, each producing one item of evidence. The evidence items for one control together make its evidence pack.

entries.name: Evidence pack
entries.def: The set of evidence items that together show one control is in place: for example a register, a record and an approval. Each item is a file you keep in 02_Working and cite by its Evidence ref.

entries.name: LI-A.x.y (control task page)
entries.def: The Lead Implementer task page for one Annex A control: what the control requires, its owner role and the sub-tasks that produce its evidence.

entries.name: LI-A.x.y-nn (sub-task)
entries.def: One sub-task of a control's page. Doing it produces one evidence item for that control.

entries.name: LI-Q1 to LI-Q8 (fixed questions)
entries.def: The eight fixed questions a Lead Implementer asks about every control in a sprint, each with where to look for its answer.
entries.where: Learn › Reference pages › LI-Q fixed questions

entries.name: RV-Q1 to RV-Q8 (review questions)
entries.def: The eight questions a reviewer asks of each card of the Review Deck, and where each answer is found.

entries.name: LI-nn (Lead Implementer extension)
entries.def: One of the 18 extensions of the ISO/IEC 27001 Lead Implementer track. Each adds one deliverable to a core task, with its own template and reference pages.
entries.where: Task card; Lead Implementer course table

entries.name: Lead Implementer track (LI)
entries.def: The part of the programme that practises what an ISO/IEC 27001 Lead Implementer does: setting up and running an information security management system. Its deliverables carry codes that start with LI.

entries.name: Deliverable code (IR-TTX, DEC-LOG)
entries.def: The code of a file or form you hand in with a task. The task card lists each one with its format.

entries.name: Template code (T-LI-CIT, T-ROPA)
entries.def: A ready-made file or frame that your deliverable starts from. The task step says which one to open and which sheet or columns to fill.
entries.where: 01_Inputs of the task; Learn › Sentence frames

entries.name: Dataset (SOA-93, TTX, VUL-40)
entries.def: A table of synthetic (made-up) records that a task gives you to work on. Its name says what it holds; its rows have IDs you cite as evidence.

entries.name: Row ID (VUL-0031, FW-1000, A-HQ-07)
entries.def: The label of one row in a dataset: a short prefix and a number. You cite it as an Evidence ref so anyone can find the row again.

entries.name: NC-1 (a nonconformity's number)
entries.def: The number of one nonconformity in an audit's findings, so the response can say which finding it answers.

entries.name: SEV1 to SEV4 (severity)
entries.def: The severity scale for incidents: SEV1 (Critical) is the worst and SEV4 (Low) the mildest, ranked by impact on safety, service, data, money and reputation. Use the scale in the incident policy, not your own feeling.

entries.name: TTX (tabletop exercise)
entries.def: A tabletop exercise is a rehearsal of an incident held around a table: a scenario is read out in stages (injects), and the team says what it would do at each. No system is touched.

entries.name: Inject (INJ-3)
entries.def: One new piece of news dropped into a tabletop exercise at a set time, such as an alert or a call. The group has to react to it before the next one arrives.

entries.name: IR (incident response)
entries.def: Incident response is how an organisation spots, contains, investigates and recovers from a security incident, and learns from it. IRC is the Incident Response & Crisis Manager role.

entries.name: Post-incident review
entries.def: A written look back after an incident: what happened, how it was handled and what to change. It records facts, not blame.

entries.name: BIA (business impact analysis)
entries.def: A business impact analysis finds which services matter most and how fast each must be back after a disruption. It is where the RTO and RPO come from.

entries.name: RTO (recovery time objective)
entries.def: How long a service may be down before the damage becomes unacceptable. It is the target for getting the service back.

entries.name: RPO (recovery point objective)
entries.def: How much recent data an organisation can afford to lose, measured as time: an RPO of four hours means the latest backup may be at most four hours old.

entries.name: DR (disaster recovery)
entries.def: Disaster recovery is the plan and the technology for getting IT services working again after a major failure. A DR test proves the plan by trying it.

entries.name: BCM / BCP / BC (business continuity)
entries.def: Business continuity is keeping the important work of the organisation going, or restoring it quickly, when something goes wrong. A BCP is the written plan for it.

entries.name: SOC (security operations centre)
entries.def: The team that watches an organisation's systems for attacks and responds. Not to be confused with SOC 2, an assurance report.

entries.name: SIEM
entries.def: A security information and event management system collects logs from many systems in one place and raises alerts when they show something suspicious.

entries.name: DLP (data loss prevention)
entries.def: Tools and rules that spot sensitive data leaving where it should stay, such as a customer list sent to a personal e-mail, and warn or block it.

entries.name: EDR (endpoint detection and response)
entries.def: Software on laptops and servers that watches for malicious behaviour and lets the security team isolate a device.

entries.name: UTC and time zones (UTC, Manila UTC+8)
entries.def: UTC is the world's reference time and does not change with the seasons. Manila is eight hours ahead of UTC (UTC+8): to turn a UTC time into Manila time, add 8 hours, and watch for the date moving on.

entries.name: MFA (multi-factor authentication)
entries.def: Signing in with two or more different proofs, such as a password and a code from a phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

entries.name: SSO (single sign-on)
entries.def: One sign-in that opens many applications, so access can be given and removed in one place.

entries.name: IAM (identity and access management)
entries.def: The processes and tools that decide who has an account and what each account may do. In the case study the IAM team is the group that changes accounts.

entries.name: PAM (privileged access management)
entries.def: Extra control over powerful accounts, such as administrators: who may use them, when, and a record of what they did.

entries.name: Privileged account
entries.def: An account that can change systems or see everything, such as an administrator. It needs tighter checks than an ordinary account.

entries.name: SoD (segregation of duties)
entries.def: One person must not hold two roles that together allow fraud or error to go unnoticed, such as raising a payment and approving it.

entries.name: UAR (user access review)
entries.def: A periodic check that each person's access is still needed and approved, with leavers and unused accounts removed.

entries.name: VPN
entries.def: A virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel that lets someone reach the company network safely from outside.

entries.name: VLAN
entries.def: A way of splitting one physical network into separate virtual networks, so a problem in one part does not reach the rest.

entries.name: TLS / HTTPS / HTTP
entries.def: TLS encrypts traffic between two computers. HTTPS is the web (HTTP) carried over TLS; plain HTTP is not encrypted.

entries.name: SSH / RDP / FTP / SMB / SMTP / NTP / DNS / LDAP
entries.def: Network protocols and terms. In short: SSH and RDP are remote-admin access; FTP and SMB move files; SMTP sends e-mail; NTP sets clocks; DNS turns names into addresses; LDAP is a directory of accounts; RADIUS checks network logins; NAC controls which devices join a network.

entries.name: API
entries.def: A set of rules that lets one program ask another for data or actions. A weak API can expose data the web page would not.

entries.name: PKI / HSM / KMS / certificates
entries.def: Cryptography terms. PKI issues and manages digital certificates; an HSM or KMS keeps encryption keys safe; AES is a standard way to encrypt data; RSA and ECDSA are ways to sign and exchange keys; FIDO2 is passwordless sign-in with a security key.

entries.name: CAB / RFC (change control)
entries.def: A change advisory board approves changes to systems; an RFC (request for change) is the record asking for one. Change control makes sure changes are approved, tested and recorded.

entries.name: SDLC (secure development life cycle)
entries.def: The stages software goes through from idea to retirement, with security checks built into each stage.

entries.name: SBOM
entries.def: A software bill of materials: the list of components inside a piece of software, so a flaw in one can be traced.

entries.name: CVSS
entries.def: A 0 to 10 score of how severe a vulnerability is. Higher is worse; the policy sets how fast each band must be fixed.

entries.name: KEV (known exploited vulnerabilities)
entries.def: A public list, kept by the US CISA, of vulnerabilities that attackers are known to be using. A KEV listing makes a finding more urgent.

entries.name: Vulnerability and patch
entries.def: A vulnerability is a weakness an attacker could use. A patch is the vendor's fix for it.

entries.name: ICT
entries.def: Information and communication technology: computers, networks, software and telephony.

entries.name: SaaS / UCaaS / CRM / ERP / WFM
entries.def: Common system types. SaaS is software rented over the internet; UCaaS is phone and meeting tools the same way; a CRM holds customer records; an ERP runs finance and operations; a WFM schedules staff; a PBX or VoIP system carries calls; a UPS keeps power on briefly; OT and ICS are the machines that run physical processes.

entries.name: CSPM / UEBA / APT / BYOD
entries.def: CSPM checks cloud settings for mistakes; UEBA spots unusual user behaviour; an APT is a patient, well-resourced attacker; BYOD means staff use their own devices for work.

entries.name: ISMS (information security management system)
entries.def: The set of policies, processes, roles and records an organisation uses to manage information security as a continuing system, as ISO/IEC 27001 requires.

entries.name: ISO/IEC 27001:2022
entries.def: The international standard that sets out what an information security management system must do. Clauses 4 to 10 are the requirements an organisation is certified against; Annex A lists 93 controls.

entries.name: ISO/IEC 27002:2022
entries.def: The companion standard that explains each Annex A control in detail: its purpose and how to apply it. It is guidance, not a certification standard.

entries.name: Annex A
entries.def: The list of 93 information security controls in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, in four themes: organisational (A.5), people (A.6), physical (A.7) and technological (A.8).

entries.name: Control
entries.def: Something an organisation does or has in place to reduce a risk: a rule, a check, a tool.

entries.name: Annex A control (A.5.24)
entries.def: One control of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A. The first number is the theme (5 organisational, 6 people, 7 physical, 8 technological).

entries.name: Clause (4.1 to 10.2)
entries.def: A numbered requirement of the main text of ISO/IEC 27001, from clause 4 (context) to clause 10 (improvement). An organisation must meet all of them to be certified.

entries.name: SoA (Statement of Applicability)
entries.def: The document listing all 93 Annex A controls, saying for each whether it applies, why, and whether it is in place. ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 requires it.

entries.name: PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act)
entries.def: The improvement cycle behind ISO management systems: Plan what to do, Do it, Check the results, Act on what the check found, then go round again. ISO/IEC 27001's clauses follow it.

entries.name: ISMS scope
entries.def: The boundary of the ISMS: which locations, services, systems and people it covers and which it does not (clause 4.3).

entries.name: Interested party
entries.def: A person or body that is affected by, or cares about, the organisation's information security: customers, regulators, staff, suppliers. Clause 4.2 asks for their requirements.

entries.name: Maturity level
entries.def: A 1 to 5 rating of how well a practice is run, from Level 1 (ad hoc) up to Level 5 (continually optimised). You work out a level by asking the Maturity Model's questions in order and stopping at the first No.

entries.name: Status (control status)
entries.def: Where a control stands today, as the rule L13 words it. Status and maturity level are separate questions: status says what is in place, level says how well it is run.

entries.name: Documented information
entries.def: ISO's phrase for the policies, procedures and records an ISMS must keep and control (clause 7.5).

entries.name: ISMS objectives
entries.def: What the organisation wants its ISMS to achieve, each with an owner, a date and a way of checking it (clause 6.2).

entries.name: Evidence ref
entries.def: The source of a value: a document and section, or a dataset row ID. Every value you enter needs one, so someone else can check it.

entries.name: 00_Admin, 01_Inputs, 02_Working, 03_Submission
entries.def: Your platform folders for a task: 00_Admin for your own records, 01_Inputs for the files you are given, 02_Working for your drafts and evidence, 03_Submission for what you hand in.

entries.name: W01 to W12 (week folder)
entries.def: The folder for one week of the programme in your workspace, for example W08 for week 8.

entries.name: Mentee ID
entries.def: Your own identifier on the platform. It starts every folder path and is on your records.

entries.name: Decision step
entries.def: A step that gives you a situation and options and asks you to choose one. About half of each task is decisions; the rest are numbered instructions.

entries.name: Tech Lab
entries.def: Five required hands-on simulators under Systems. Each shows a made-up system's screens; you capture evidence of problems and record your findings, which the task's hand-in needs.

entries.name: Tech Lab scenario ID (TL-36-…)
entries.def: The identifier of one Tech Lab scenario: the organisation it belongs to, its area and its number.

entries.name: PBC (Prepared By Client)
entries.def: A request list of the documents an auditor asks the organisation to provide before or during an audit.

entries.name: Evidence
entries.def: A record that proves something was done or is in place, such as a log, a signed approval or a configuration export. It must be dated, attributable and unaltered.

entries.name: Manifest
entries.def: A receipt of what you handed in, listing each file with its hash and the UTC time.

entries.name: SHA-256 (file hash)
entries.def: A fixed-length fingerprint calculated from a file's contents. If even one character changes, the fingerprint changes, so it proves a file was not altered.

entries.name: RR / risk register
entries.def: The list of an organisation's risks, each with a rating, an owner, a treatment and a status. RR-UPD is your updated copy of it.

entries.name: Risk
entries.def: The chance that something goes wrong and the harm if it does. Risks are written as a cause, an event and an effect and rated by likelihood and impact.

entries.name: Residual risk
entries.def: The risk that remains after controls and treatment are applied.

entries.name: Risk appetite
entries.def: How much risk an organisation is willing to carry without treating it further. Scores above that line need a decision from the right person.

entries.name: Risk treatment
entries.def: What is done about a risk: reduce it with controls, avoid it, share it (insurance or a supplier) or accept it. The treatment plan lists the choice, the controls, the owner and the date.

entries.name: Risk assessment method (RAM)
entries.def: The rules an organisation uses to assess risk the same way every time: the scales, the criteria and who accepts what.

entries.name: Asset–threat–control chain
entries.def: A way of writing a risk by linking what you protect (the asset), what could harm it (the threat) and what is in place against it (the control).

entries.name: Asset
entries.def: Anything of value to the organisation that needs protecting: information, systems, people, premises.

entries.name: Threat
entries.def: Something that could cause harm to an asset, such as an attacker, a failure or a mistake.

entries.name: Exception
entries.def: A case where a control did not work as the rule says, or where a rule was knowingly set aside with approval.

entries.name: KPI / KRI
entries.def: A key performance indicator measures how well something is working against a target; a key risk indicator warns that a risk is rising. Both are numbers with a target and a date.

entries.name: SLA (service level agreement)
entries.def: A promise about how fast or how well something will be done, such as fixing a critical vulnerability within a set number of days.

entries.name: RACI
entries.def: A chart giving each activity four kinds of role: Responsible (does it), Accountable (answers for it), Consulted (asked first) and Informed (told afterwards).

entries.name: Gap analysis
entries.def: Comparing what an organisation does today with what a standard asks, and listing what is missing.

entries.name: Obligations register
entries.def: A list of the legal and contractual duties that apply to an organisation, with who owns each and how it is met.

entries.name: NC (nonconformity), major and minor
entries.def: A requirement of the standard or of the ISMS that was not met. An auditor grades it major or minor; ISO/IEC 27001 clause 10.2 says how it must be corrected.

entries.name: OFI (opportunity for improvement)
entries.def: An auditor's note about something that meets the requirement but could be better. It is not a nonconformity and needs no corrective action.

entries.name: Corrective action
entries.def: What is done to fix a nonconformity and stop it happening again: the correction deals with the problem found, the corrective action deals with its root cause.

entries.name: Internal audit and management review
entries.def: An internal audit checks, on a plan, that the ISMS meets the standard and the organisation's own rules (clause 9.2). A management review is the periodic meeting where top management reviews how the ISMS is performing (clause 9.3).

entries.name: Stage 1 and Stage 2 audit
entries.def: The two parts of a certification audit. Stage 1 reviews the documents and readiness; Stage 2 checks on site that the ISMS is really in use and works.

entries.name: Certification body
entries.def: The independent organisation, accredited to do so, that audits an organisation against ISO/IEC 27001 and decides whether to certify it. IAF is the body that links national accreditation bodies; PECB and BSI are examples of training and certification organisations.

entries.name: Sampling
entries.def: Checking a selected part of a large set (some records or some changes) and drawing a conclusion about the whole. The sampling table says how many to take.

entries.name: SOC 1 / SOC 2 / CUEC
entries.def: SOC reports are independent auditors' reports on a service provider's controls. CUECs are the controls the provider expects its customers to run themselves.

entries.name: NIST CSF / CIS / SANS / GIAC / GCIH
entries.def: Frameworks and bodies named in the pack. NIST CSF and the CIS Controls are security frameworks; SANS and GIAC give security training and certificates; CISA is the US cybersecurity agency; CFR is the US Code of Federal Regulations.

entries.name: GDPR
entries.def: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation: the law on how personal data of people in the EU may be collected, used and kept.

entries.name: PII (personal data)
entries.def: Information that identifies a person, directly or together with other data. It needs more protection than other data.

entries.name: DPIA (data protection impact assessment)
entries.def: An assessment done before a new use of personal data that could put people at high risk, to find and reduce the privacy risk first.

entries.name: RoPA (record of processing activities)
entries.def: A record, required by the GDPR, of what personal data an organisation processes, why, who gets it and how long it is kept.

entries.name: DPA (data processing agreement / Data Privacy Act)
entries.def: Usually a data processing agreement: the contract that sets what a supplier may do with the organisation's personal data. In the Philippines, DPA 2012 is the Data Privacy Act.

entries.name: DPO (Data Protection Officer)
entries.def: The person responsible for advising on and watching over an organisation's compliance with data protection law.

entries.name: Regulators and privacy laws named in the pack
entries.def: Laws and regulators of the offices in the case study. For example the NPC is the Philippines' privacy regulator; KVKK and the UAVG are Turkish and Dutch privacy laws; HIPAA covers US health data; PCI DSS covers payment cards; DOLE is the Philippine labour department; the NBI issues Philippine clearance certificates.

entries.name: AML / KYC
entries.def: Anti-money-laundering rules, and know-your-customer checks, the identity checks financial services must run on their customers.

entries.name: NDA / MSA / DPA clauses
entries.def: A non-disclosure agreement keeps shared information secret; a master services agreement sets the general terms between a customer and a supplier.

entries.name: ISAC
entries.def: An information sharing and analysis centre: a sector group whose members share news of threats and attacks.

entries.name: TPRM (third-party risk management)
entries.def: Managing the risk that comes from suppliers and partners who handle your data or services.

entries.name: Vendor tier and contract checklist
entries.def: A vendor's tier says how much oversight it needs; the contract clause checklist records whether its contract holds the clauses the Group requires.

entries.name: Role abbreviations
entries.def: A GRC role of the Group, shown by its short code. The longer name is on the task card.

entries.name: CEO / CIO / CFO / CHRO / CRCO / CPM
entries.def: Management roles: the chief executive, chief information, chief financial and chief human resources officers; CRCO is the organisation's chief risk and compliance officer and CPM the Cybersecurity Program Manager.

entries.name: CISO
entries.def: The Chief Information Security Officer: the executive who leads the organisation's information security.

entries.name: HR / IT / QA / BPO / KPO
entries.def: Everyday business abbreviations: HR is human resources, IT is the technology team, QA is quality assurance, a BPO or KPO is a company that runs another company's processes, HQ is head office and RO a regional office.

entries.name: Org A and Org B (your two organisations)
entries.def: You work for two fictional organisations all programme. Org A is GlobalConnect Customer Solutions in Manila; Org B is LearnTech Educational Solutions in Amsterdam. The names you see are yours.

entries.name: SITL (the Group)
entries.def: The fictional group that owns the policies and runs the programme. Its documents carry the prefix SITL.

entries.name: SITL document (SITL-POL-014)
entries.def: A policy, standard or addendum of the Group. POL is a policy, STD a standard, ERM the risk framework, ADD an organisation's addendum and TSA its technology stack and assets sheet.

entries.name: RA and TSA sheets
entries.def: The risk assessment (RA) and technology stack and assets (TSA) workbooks for each organisation, listing its registered assets and systems.

entries.name: Reference pack
entries.def: The set of documents, datasets and templates the programme gives you. Everything you need to answer a step is in it.

entries.name: Physical walkthrough (PHY-WALK)
entries.def: A walk through the premises with a checklist, looking at doors, rooms, badges and equipment, and recording what you see.

entries.name: Configuration baseline
entries.def: The agreed secure settings for a system. A baseline check compares the actual settings with them.

entries.name: Awareness plan
entries.def: A plan for teaching staff about security, with themes, audiences and dates. SAT is the Security Awareness & Training Specialist role.

entries.name: Topic-specific policy
entries.def: A policy on one subject, such as access control or backup, beneath the main information security policy (Annex A 5.1).

entries.name: Action tracker
entries.def: A list of actions with an owner, a due date and a status, used to follow findings through to closure.

entries.name: Measurement dashboard
entries.def: A one-page view of the measures the ISMS tracks, each with its value, target and threshold.

entries.name: Method code (G.i, D.ii)
entries.def: A code from the programme's list of GRC methods: a letter for the group of methods and a roman numeral for the method, followed by its name. It says which kind of GRC work a task practises.

entries.name: NIST CSF subcategory (DE.CM-01)
entries.def: A numbered outcome of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: two letters for the function, two for the category and a number, for example DE.CM-01 is in Detect.

entries.name: Template file code (FAM-MAP, CTX-BRIEF)
entries.def: The name of the working file a template opens, as the task step calls it.

entries.name: Lead Implementer extension codes
entries.def: Codes of Lead Implementer deliverables or feedback files named in the programme's course table: LI-PLAN is the plan and objectives sheet, LI-IRBC the incident-response and continuity extension, LI-CHG the change-planning extension and CLI-FB the corrective-action feedback file.

entries.name: GRC (governance, risk and compliance)
entries.def: Governance (who decides and how), risk (what could go wrong) and compliance (meeting laws, standards and promises) treated as one discipline. It is the work of this programme.

entries.name: CA / VM / VUL / CT (system and dataset terms)
entries.def: CA is a certificate authority, the service that issues digital certificates; a VM is a virtual machine; CRQ is the call-recording and QA platform of the case study; a TR is a test run; VUL is the vulnerability-scan dataset and CT the change-ticket dataset (CT-B is its variant B).

entries.name: COPC / ERM / SSAP / CX / OSPO
entries.def: Terms named in the pack. COPC is a customer-experience standard for contact centres; ERM is enterprise risk management; SSAP is a SANS awareness credential; CX is customer experience; OSPO is an open-source programme office; CEFR is the European scale of language levels; PESTLE and SWOT are frameworks for describing context; an SOP is a standard operating procedure.

entries.name: Charter role ID (OG-CISO, PD-IRM-001)
entries.def: The identifier of a role in the Group GRC Charter's role list.

entries.name: Date formats (DD-MMM-YYYY, YYYY-MM-DD)
entries.def: DD-MMM-YYYY is a date written day, month name, year (05-Oct-2026). YYYY-MM-DD is the year-first form used in file names and stored values (2026-10-05).

entries.name: Annex numbering (A.7)
entries.def: A.7 is the physical-controls group of Annex A. CLD.6.3.1 is a control of the cloud-services guidance ISO/IEC 27017.

entries.name: Read first / Sources for this step
entries.def: The card at the top of a step that names where its facts and rules are: a document section, a rule, a reference page, a dataset. Each one opens beside your work at the part to read. It names the place and never the answer.

entries.name: Save to 02_Working
entries.def: The button on a task's last step. It puts the finished file in your 02_Working folder and marks the step done. It does not hand the task in: that is Submit task.

entries.name: Submit task (seal)
entries.def: Handing a whole task in, once every step is done. The desk asks you to confirm first, because a submitted task is sealed: it is scored and you cannot change it afterwards.

entries.name: Check my answer (lock)
entries.def: Pressing Check my answer compares what you chose with the key and locks it: what you chose at that moment is what is scored. In the first weeks the desk asks you to confirm before it locks.

entries.name: Office entry
entries.def: A value the office filled in before you arrived, shown in grey until you have checked it. It is not your answer and it may be wrong: checking it against the source is the step.

entries.name: Score breakdown (How this score was made)
entries.def: The list under a submitted task's score on My Submissions and Reports: each checked decision, Inbox reply and table of picks, the points it carried, the points you earned, and the rule behind each loss.

entries.name: Written cell and the marking guide
entries.def: A cell you fill with your own sentence, such as a reason or a next action. It is checked for its format only and kept with your hand-in; no person or model reads it, and it adds or removes no points. The Guide's marking section shows a good one and a weak one.

entries.name: Hazard profile (natural-hazard and climate profile)
entries.def: The table in Section 1 of each organisation's addendum that lists, office by office, the country's natural-hazard score, its principal hazards and what the office itself has recorded. The scores are those of SITL-ERM-001 Annex B.

entries.name: Framework Quick Reference
entries.def: The list under Learn that says, in our own words, what each clause and the main controls of ISO/IEC 27001 ask for. It is a summary to find your way: read the standard itself before citing it.
